en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Siming in the Song Dynasty.
II. Regarding the section "Successive Order" (*krama*) below, this clarifies the sequence of the chapters; it has two parts: first, clarifying where all the chapters converge.
This is also the underlying purpose for the introduction of this present chapter. Regarding the section beginning with "What is it?", it explains the sequence of the various chapters.

As for the statement that the "Introductory Chapter" (序品) describes the "Great Essence" (大體), the preceding commentary explained that the sutra describes five topics; yet here, only the "Essence" is described because it refers to the ultimate fruit—the sphere in which one dwells and the reality with which one accords—which is sublime and vast. This *dharmatā* (法性), realized at the stage of Buddhahood, constitutes the Great Essence of the present sutra.
From the "Life Span" chapter down to the various chapters on merit, none of them transcend great wisdom and its great function.

As for the phrase "exhausting the source," it means that within the state of wondrous enlightenment, the source of principle has been fully exhausted and the limits of phenomena have also been reached; thus, the all-encompassing wisdom merges with its illumination and the myriad practices come to rest. This is the single nature with no other path, and therefore it is called the fundamental substance of the sutra.

In the "Life Span" chapter, the two wisdoms of the stage of fruition are already perfected; thus, while they merge with the profound and vast essence, they give rise to functions of both long and short duration. How could the guidance provided by the "Repentance," "Praise," and "Emptiness" chapters ever exceed these great functions?
The merits described in all chapters correspond to the essential substance without contradiction; therefore, it is stated below that "all are due to the power of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
From the words "In this way" onwards, there are two parts: second, showing the intent of the praise in the present text.
This explains that because of the benefits derived from the preceding seventeen chapters, there are the eulogistic verses of the subsequent sixty-two lines.

Regarding "making a good beginning and a good end": since the three sections, beginning with the Prologue, have all attained their respective benefits, the three Bodhisattvas, bearing the Buddha’s profound kindness upon their shoulders, offer praise; thus, there is the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha," which likewise constitutes a good conclusion.
Third, the explanation of the text, in two parts:
first, the presentation of the outline;
second, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts.
First, the introduction by the sūtra compiler;
the commentary (*śāstra*) is clear on this point.
The sūtra states, "From here to the kingdom of Suvarṇaprabhāsa," intending to magnify the assembly, showing that all the bodhisattvas therein praise the Teacher Śākyamuni.
Recently, I have observed some who do not understand this principle and claim that [this passage] praises that Buddha.
The commentaries on the sutras are by no means obscure; how can one be so ignorant?
Fearing that later students might follow such interpretations and erroneously explain the scriptural text, I shall now briefly cite the commentary to demonstrate it.

Regarding the origin of the "Chapter on Praise": it is because the three Bodhisattvas all benefited from hearing the sutra above, and thus praised the Buddha and his teaching; how could this concern any other Buddha?

Moreover, the Commentary states: "One Buddha is the one who praises. If it is claimed that this refers to praising that [other] Buddha, why would the one who praises that single Buddha necessarily be identified as Śākyamuni?
The commentary on the sutra is clear and lucid; therefore, I shall not cite it at length.
Second, the actual explanation of the verses, in two parts:
first, the detailed analysis and explanation of the text’s divisions. Second...
First, the division of the text.
That is, the Master Zhi (Zhiyi) divided the verses according to the title; thus, he combined the sixty-five and a half lines of text into three sections.

He included the three lines of scripture concerning the Tathāgata’s emergence from meditative concentration within the section on the tree deity. Therefore, it is said that "the tree deity speaks for twenty-eight and a half lines."
The textual divisions are clearly visible, yet the *Śāstra* does not explain them in detail; therefore, the commentary provides the following notes.
It should be stated that the sixty-five lines and a half of text are divided into two parts:

first, sixty-two lines and a half consisting of three successive expositions by the Bodhisattvas; second, the final three lines consisting of the exposition by the Tathāgata upon arising from meditative concentration.
Therefore, the subsequent chapter provides a general explanation, stating: "Its text consists of four parts," which is precisely this meaning, as detailed below in the commentary.
Second, the explanation of the meaning, in three parts.
However, these three sections of the Bodhisattva’s praise are not analyzed in the Commentary; those who have attained mastery will surely find both the words and their meaning clear.
Fearing that beginners may not understand, I shall now provide a brief structural analysis and explanation.
First, the praise by the bodhisattvas, in three parts:
First, praise expressed through words, in three parts:
First, praise of the virtues of the teaching master’s own practice, in three parts:
First, the praise of the ocean of major and minor marks, in two parts:
first, the single line beginning with "Tathāgata" praises the one major mark of golden light.
The phrase "the body of the Tathāgata" serves as the introductory heading.
The three phrases beginning with "Golden-colored, subtle, and so forth" praise the fourteenth major mark, the subtle golden-hued light.
Second, the two and a half lines beginning with "Pure body" praise the three minor marks, such as the cleanliness of the body.
The Sūtra states that "purity of body" praises the eleventh minor mark, the cleanliness of the body;
"softness" praises the twelfth minor mark, the softness of the body.
The two phrases "perfectly complete" and "stainless" praise the twentieth minor mark (*anuvyañjana*), the fulfillment of the body, and also praise the perfection of his deportment.

Third, the two lines beginning with "His voice" re-praise the one major mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the Brahma-voice, and also concurrently praise the ocean of minor marks such as the profound and far-reaching quality of his speech.
The Brahma-voice is a metaphor for the Buddha’s voice being profound and far-reaching;
the lion’s roar is a metaphor for the Buddha’s voice being fearless;
the sound of a great thunderclap is a metaphor for the Buddha’s voice shattering delusion.

Regarding what are called the six kinds of voice, all texts state there are eight qualities: first, extremely beautiful; second, soft and supple; third, harmonious and appropriate; fourth, noble and wise; fifth, not feminine; sixth, unerring; seventh, deep and far-reaching; eighth, inexhaustible.
Regarding variations in length caused by the translator, there is no need for reconciliation.
Alternatively, one may first cite "wondrous like the Brahma-voice," which refers to the "deep and far-reaching voice" among the eight qualities of speech.
"Lion’s roar" and "great thunderous resonance" refer to the "non-feminine voice."

Because the Buddha abides in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and constantly possesses the virtues of a World Hero, having long since abandoned the feminine and weak mind, the sounds he utters cause all who hear them to feel awe and reverence; thus, none among the celestial Māras or non-Buddhist paths fail to submit and take refuge.

Since two types of sounds have already been listed above, the mention below of "six types of sounds" refers specifically to the six sounds such as those of the kalaviṅka and the peacock; for *kalaviṅka* is translated as "exceedingly beautiful sound."
2. The following one and a half lines, beginning with "Pure" (qingjing), praise the sublime marks of the Honored One.
Above, the praise was given by alternating between the large and the small; this is intended to reveal that both the large and small bodily marks are all-pervasive.

Although the meaning was contained within the phrasing, the *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (the unique, preeminent marks) had not yet been fully revealed; therefore, it is now further praised that both the physical marks and the radiance are limitless and boundless.
What the Sūtra calls "majestic virtue" (*pratāpa*) refers to the appearance of one who is lofty, dignified, and magnificent.

2. The two lines beginning with "wisdom" praise the merits of his knowledge and abandonment; the first line praises the merit of his knowledge, while the second line praises the merit of his abandonment.
3. The section beginning with "World-Honored One" summarizes his preeminent excellence.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "As for the Buddha of the Universal Body (*vairocana-kāya*), he is majestic and sublime; like Mount Sumeru towering over the great ocean, all his major and minor marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*) are likewise majestic and sublime."

"However, while the Tathāgata himself fully possesses the merits of the three bodies, when the bodhisattvas praise only the Honored One with the Extraordinary Marks, they have already encompassed the three bodies through the principle of the upper [principle] merging with the lower [phenomena] and the lower responding to the upper."
This is a praise of the skillfulness of wisdom; let students reflect upon it.
Second, the six and a half lines beginning with "For the sake of all" praise the benefit of transforming others through the teaching that was expounded, in two parts:
first, an account of the causes and conditions for expounding the teaching.
This is evident in the text.
The new sutra states: "In order to benefit all sentient beings, one constantly practices the gift of Dharma, even to the point of enabling them to attain the great fruit and realize eternal bliss."
2. Praising the Taught Dharma, in two parts:
First, the two phrases beginning with "Tathāgata" praise the essential body (*śarīra*) of the sūtra.

"Body" refers to that wherein the Tathāgata dwells as described in the "Introductory Chapter": profound and vast, without boundaries, and transcending all causal principles; therefore, it is called the "supreme profound meaning."
"Raising the profound to encompass the vast" refers to the extremely deep and immeasurable.
The essential purport points to the ultimate fruit attained in the "Life Span" chapter, which surpasses all bodhisattvas and is likewise called the foremost.
The identity of the Dharma-body and the Reward-body can be understood through this profound meaning.
Second, praising the power and function of the sutra, in three parts:
first, the two lines beginning with "able to cause" praise the eradication of evil in the preceding "Chapter on Repentance."
"Quiescence" means the stilling of the evils of karmic actions and the extinction of the suffering of their retributive fruits.
Second, the two lines beginning with "capable of bestowing" praise the generation of wholesome roots in the preceding "Chapter on Praise."

The above is the Tathāgata’s narration of the past and the Dragon King’s praise of the Buddha; because it gives rise to the wholesome conditions appropriate for the present occasion, it is able to bestow immeasurable happiness.
Third, the praise of the "Chapter on Emptiness" as a dual guidance has two parts.
First, the single line beginning with "Able to expound" praises the subtlety of the guiding Dharma of emptiness.
The term "ambrosia" (*amṛta*) in the sutras refers to the medicine of longevity and immortality.

This text elucidates the Middle Way—the wondrous emptiness, the true reality, and the ultimate truth—which can transcend the two types of death and the deluded transformations of existence, and can give rise to the eternal body endowed with the four virtues; therefore, this principle of emptiness is called ambrosia.
Nevertheless, because the essence of defilement is fundamentally pure, it is termed the "wondrous Dharma" (*saddharma*); entering from this point is further termed a "Dharma-gate.
Second, the following two lines, beginning with "The ability to enter," praise the profundity of extinguishing evil and generating goodness.
When one attains this emptiness through repentance, the retribution for the afflictions of the two deaths immediately ceases, and one may enter the abode of the Nirvana of the Three Virtues.
Regarding what is called "liberation," there are two meanings:
if it refers to being liberated from the bonds of delusion and karma, it is the destruction of evil; [if it refers to the attainment of the fruit, it is the realization of goodness].
If one grasps the purity of uncontaminated mastery, it is the arising of the wholesome;
thus, it should be understood that by transcending the three realms of existence and so forth, evil is destroyed and the wholesome is produced.
Third, regarding the concluding praise of the person and the Dharma: "Virtue and wisdom" concludes the preceding praise of the Honored and Sublime Teacher who is the master of exposition.
"Compassion and diligence" concludes the praise for the profundity of the teachings expounded above.
That the fundamental application of the Dharma is such as this is entirely due to compassion and diligence.
2. Praise Beyond Words, in three parts:
First, the single line beginning with "Thus immeasurable... expresses praise beyond words; therefore, it cannot be measured, calculated, or illustrated by analogy.
2. The two lines beginning with "The devas and people of the world" express praise that transcends the ordinary mind;
thus, even if one exhausts all thought to measure it, one cannot know even a single drop of the great ocean, let alone a small portion thereof.
3. "I now briefly praise... (one line): This refers to the extensive concluding praise, as can be seen.
3. "If my merit... (one line): Having completed the praise, this is the dedication of merit.
There are three meanings of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), while the extant text contains two; the underlying principle encompasses all three, as can be seen from the text itself.
Second, the explanation by Śraddhālakṣaṇa has two parts:
first, the narration by the sūtra compiler.
Second, the actual verses of praise, in two parts:
first, the single line beginning with "World-Honored One" generally praises the merit of the marks and signs.
"In thousands" refers to a large number.
2. Specific Praise of the Ocean of Major and Minor Marks (five sections):
First, specific praise of the two kinds of radiant marks (two sub-sections).
First, the four lines beginning with "Purity of Color" praise the mark of color endowed with radiance.
The passage beginning with "The purity of his form shines afar" refers to the fourteenth mark, the Golden-Hued Radiance.
The passage beginning with "His light is blazing and intense" refers to the fifteenth mark, the Body-Radiance.

However, regarding the characteristics of these two kinds of light, if one refers to the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), they all have fixed limits; as it is said, "the radiance of the body extends one *zhang* in every direction.

Now, it is said that [this light] is like the thousand rays of the sun, even reaching to illuminate immeasurable Buddha-lands from afar. Thus we know that in the past, Xinxiang was a dragon king who praised the Buddha’s sublime marks (*vyañjana*) and made a vow to meet Śākyamuni in the future.
Praising the Buddha today, how could one forget his origin?
Thus, both the major and minor marks are all praised by way of relying upon the *vairocana* (exalted) form.
Second, the line beginning with "capable of extinguishing" clarifies the endowment of light and its extraction.

In the past, as the Honored Dragon, he praised the Buddha’s body for emitting great rays of light that extinguished all sufferings throughout the triple world and caused all sentient beings to experience complete happiness.
Today, in praising the Buddha, he again praises the radiance that extinguishes suffering and bestows bliss; this is evident in the text.
2. The single line beginning with "The various faculties" (*indriya*) offers a general praise of the characteristics of the faculties and the marks of physical excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

For instance, among the major marks, there are those such as a body that is upright, skin that is thin and delicate, a large tongue that covers the face, teeth that are white, even, and closely set, eyes like the essence of gold, and eyelashes like those of a bull king; and among the minor marks, there are those such as a high and well-formed nose with invisible nostrils, earlobes with well-formed spokes and ridges, and a body that is clean and soft. All these faculties leave those who behold them never satiated.
Third, furthermore, there are two parts to the comparison and praise of one minor mark (*anuvyañjana*):
first, the single line beginning with "hair dark blue" praises the mark of the hair.

The neck of a peacock, the king of bees, and so forth are all compared to the hair for their dark blue color, as seen in the eighty secondary marks (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*) such as the mark of the hair being like a blue gem.
2. The following one and a half lines, beginning with "Pure" (清淨), describe the possession of merit.
Because he has long adorned himself with pure compassion and immeasurable meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), his hair is beautiful and soft.
Fourth, further elucidating the merit of the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), in two parts:
first, elucidating the merit of possessing the marks and signs, in two parts.
First, the single line beginning with "marks and signs" clarifies the function of adorning the body and achieving the fruit; this is evident.
Second, the two lines beginning with "Tathāgata" clarify the merit of gathering sentient beings and eliciting praise.

Whether by means of the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) or the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), whether great or small, he is able to subdue them all, causing their minds to become supple and receive various forms of happiness; therefore, he is praised by all Buddhas.
Second, the two lines beginning with "Its light" clarify that his merit is endowed with radiance.
His merit is lofty and vast, like Mount Sumeru emerging from the great ocean.
5. From "The teeth are white" down to two and a half lines, there is further praise comparing the two major marks of the teeth and the *ūrṇā* hair.
3. The discourse of the tree deity, in two parts:
first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler.
Regarding what is called the Bodhi-tree deity of the site of enlightenment: this is the very place where the Tathāgata attained the Way beneath this tree.
Originally, the tree was named Pippala; however, because the Buddha sat beneath it and attained the fruit of bodhi-wisdom, this name was established for it.
Therefore, the goddess now dwells by this tree, and it is also named after her. The *Record of the Western Regions* states:
"In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, it stood several hundred feet high; though it has been repeatedly cut down, it is still forty or fifty feet tall."
Its trunk and stem are yellowish-white, while its branches and leaves are lush green; they do not wither in winter or summer, remaining radiant and unchanged.
On each anniversary of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, all the leaves fall away, only to return to their former state shortly thereafter.
This tree is located more than four hundred li southwest of the great city in the kingdom of Magadha in Central India, not far from the place where [the Buddha] practiced austerities.
2. The actual verses of praise consist of four parts;
first, two lines provide a general eulogy.
*Namo* is a term signifying taking refuge.
Regarding "purity," the *Buddhatā-śāstra* (*Foxing lun*) identifies two types:
first, purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), because it is fundamentally free from the defilement of delusions;
second, purity of appearance (*lakṣaṇa-viśuddhi*), because it is free from obstructions through the application of remedies.

Now, this is a general praise of the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom regarding the Middle and the Extremes, and the fulfillment of the Dharma, Reward, and Response bodies; therefore, it is called "Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment.
Second, the specific praise has two parts:
first, an extensive praise of the Teacher who is able to preach, in three sections:
First, the one and a half lines beginning with "Profound" (*gambhīra*) praise the Buddha’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) by way of what is awakened to.

"The profound and wondrous Dharma" refers to the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), which is lofty and vast; all phenomena are harmoniously integrated and subtle therein, and perfect wisdom and perfect awakening pervade all places.
Because all defilements and hindrances are fundamentally detached from their source, the Tathāgata accords with this principle and awakens to their true nature.

All Māras and heterodox teachers hold that *nirvāṇa* is not the Dharma and that meditation and precepts are not the Path; yet, just as a great tree with deep-rooted roots in the earth can only be uprooted by the Buddha’s unique Vajra-like Great Wisdom.
The attainment of perfect enlightenment as a Buddha refers to the Great Dharmakāya that has emerged from the entanglements.

However, according to the Perfect [Teaching], the Great Wisdom of the Buddha realizes that the original nature is neither dharma nor path; one must transcend the three vehicles and the seven expedient means. Only when Nirvāṇa is seen as not being dharma and precept, concentration, and wisdom are seen as not being the path can one be said to be far removed from all things.
"Dharma" refers to the resultant dharmas that are produced;
"Path" refers to the causal path that produces them.
If one has not yet departed from the differentiated aspects of ignorance, all such [distinctions] are said to be erroneous.
2. The two and a half lines beginning with "knowing existence" praise the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* in terms of the activity of the awakening wisdom (*bodhijñāna*). This has three parts;
first, the section concerning the Dharma.
The two lines beginning with "knowing existence" praise the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
"Knowing" means illumination.
"Existence" refers to the conventional; "non-existence" refers to the ultimate; and the intrinsically pure nature is the middle.

To know and illuminate the three truths through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is to be in profound accord with the deep and vast, reaching the ultimate limit of both phenomena and principle; this is called the Buddha’s unsurpassed retributive wisdom.
The two lines following "Rare indeed" (*āścarya*) praise the merit of the Buddha’s auxiliary practices (*sahakāri-pratipatti*).
The repetition of the word "rare" expresses a profound sense of admiration; the same applies to all subsequent instances.
Within the causal stage, the precepts, meditative concentration, and myriad practices possess the power to eliminate obstacles and counteract evil; this is termed "merit" (gong).
They assist in the arousal of great wisdom and bring about the great fruit of Buddhahood; this is termed "virtue" (de).
The *Lotus Sūtra* states, "That which is obtained through long-cultivated practice," which refers to the unsurpassed retribution; thus, it is called the merit of the Tathāgata.
Second, the line beginning with "Rare indeed" (希有) is explained by means of a metaphor.
This is a metaphor for the wisdom and practice of the aforementioned Reward Body (Sambhogakāya).
The great ocean symbolizes wisdom;
Mount Sumeru symbolizes practice.
This wisdom penetrates the profound principle and exhausts the depths of the true nature (dharmatā); therefore, it is compared to the great ocean.
The *Śāstra* states: "The great ocean of the Perfection of Wisdom—only the Buddha has exhausted its depths."

The myriad practices performed during the causal stage, accumulating merit and virtue, are likened to Mount Sumeru; as both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras state: "Even if one were to carve scriptures upon one's own bones, it would be like that Wondrous High Mountain."
3. The two lines following "Rare indeed" summarize [the preceding].
Because wisdom and practice accord with principle, and the three dharmas are identical as one, it is called "boundless practice."
3. The following one and a half lines, beginning with "Rare and Wondrous" (希有), praise the Buddha’s response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) by way of its benefits for the world through its manifested form.

As for the *udumbara* flower—its full name is *udumbarapuṣpa*; this is translated as "Auspicious Response" (*ruìyìng*), and also as "Numinous Auspice" (*língruì*). This flower appears in response to the emergence of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) into the world.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Within Jambudvīpa there is a sovereign king of trees named Udumbara; it bears fruit but has no flowers.
When the Udumbara tree bears golden flowers, a Buddha appears in the world; therefore, it is said that it manifests but once in an aeon.
"Immeasurable great compassion" refers to the manifestation of the fundamental essence.
Because of this great compassion, he does not abide in nirvana.
Second, the one and a half lines beginning with "Śākyamuni" briefly praise the Dharma teachings that were expounded.

When the Tathāgata is about to expound the Dharma through the wheel of his speech, he must first employ the mental faculty (*manas-karman*) to discern the capacities of sentient beings, just as the sun shines upon all things without exception.

For the sake of benefiting others, one should follow the power and function of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* by clearly elucidating the ten kinds of benefit; only then will the intention behind his teaching for the welfare of the world be fully realized.
III. Requesting the Buddha to emerge from meditative absorption, in two parts:
A. Praising the present meditative absorption entered as the basis for the request, in three parts:
1. The first two lines beginning with "Excellent" praise the absorption in which the Buddha of the fruit abides.

Regarding those whose faculties are tranquil: because they have realized that the nature of the eyes and other sense organs is eternal, and because they possess unimpaired cultivation, all afflictions, death, and birth have been entirely stilled; thus, they constantly abide in tranquil concentration.
Furthermore, as for "entering into [samādhi] again," it signifies that he will turn the wheel of the Dharma and demonstrates that his speech is not false.

Moreover, the Buddhas of the three periods must enter meditative concentration (samādhi) before speaking; thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Although one knows that all phenomena are eternally the mark of concentration, one nevertheless manifests to sentient beings the distinctions among various dhyānas."
The term "Great City of Excellent Tranquility" is a direct praise for the meditative concentration (samādhi) entered therein.

This refers to the *dharmatā-samādhi* mentioned at the beginning of the sutra; if one enters this concentration, one is able to thoroughly understand that all phenomena are quiescent, for there is nothing that is not the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
To prevent the errors of birth and death and to ward off the enemies of nirvāṇa, one abides in the Middle Way of sublime tranquility, which is thus named the "Great City.
It is also called the "Stainless and Pure Samādhi" and so forth; as it is the realm of the Buddha, it receives the name "Stainless and Pure."
This is the sphere of practice for all Buddhas.
Second, it clarifies the characteristics of the practice of emptiness through samādhi.
Although this sutra ultimately concludes with the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings, its exposition occurs after the period of the Prajñāpāramitā.

In this practice of repentance and praise, both good and evil are traced back to emptiness as the guiding principle; thus, the "Chapter on Emptiness" states that emptiness has already been extensively explained in countless other sutras.
For this reason, this sutra also discusses emptiness as a gateway for entering into the ultimate truth.
The Buddha’s dwelling in samādhi also enters from emptiness; yet although the śrāvakas likewise enter from emptiness, they remain entangled by the fruits of their own bodies.

Through the clear vision of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of emptiness, he perceives that the nature and characteristics of the śrāvakas’ bodily fruits are all empty, and that the realm of the Buddhas is likewise empty.

"All these immeasurable dharmas" refers to the aforementioned distinctions between self and other, cause and fruit, and the purity or defilement of lands; yet when one investigates their nature and their characteristics, no differentiation or gradation is found.
The environments and sentient beings of all living things, when their nature and characteristics are investigated, are found to be identical to true purity, with no further distinction between them.
Thus, the investigation of nature and characteristics is the essential gateway for employing the contemplation of emptiness to eliminate deluded attachments and reveal the underlying principle.

While various schools have clarified contemplation and discussed it collectively, even among those who engage in formal study, many remain obscure regarding its true nature. Our school, however, relies upon the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as its foundation; by adhering to reason and meaning, we have expanded the gateways of contemplation, thereby clarifying both the phenomenal and noumenal aspects of both provisional and ultimate teachings.
Students must understand this:

for instance, the two types of emptiness—emptiness of nature and emptiness of characteristics—are fundamentally a single method of contemplation on emptiness; they are presented as two successive stages of practice in order to thoroughly eliminate all conceptualizations and mental constructions.
Thus we know that if one skillfully cultivates the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one will necessarily eliminate two kinds of grasping at intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

As the *Lotus Sūtra* simply states, "Know that dharmas are eternally without nature," Jingxi [Zhiyi] explains this as the nature of being without nature (*asvabhāvatā-svabhāva*) and the nature of being without marks (*alakṣaṇa-svabhāva*).

The various texts distinguish between nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by resorting to sequential exposition; thus, they divide them according to the two truths (*satyadvaya*). Consequently, it is said: "When one investigates nature through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and does not perceive nature, this is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) that negates nature."
"By analyzing through the four propositions, one does not perceive the name; this is the ultimate truth that destroys characteristics.
To destroy characteristics is precisely for characteristics to be empty.
Jingxi’s commentary states:

"If there is attachment to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the world is not the truth; once attachment to intrinsic nature is destroyed, the world is then called the truth. For this reason, it is termed 'worldly truth that destroys intrinsic nature.
Once attachment to intrinsic nature is destroyed, there remains only a name, which is designated as 'conventional' (*prajñapti*)."
The provisional is itself the characteristic, because it is the characteristic of emptiness.
To contemplate principle and realize the truth is called "the ultimate truth that destroys characteristics.

Since emptiness is neither prior nor posterior and the two truths are simultaneous, one knows that although it is termed "conventional truth" once the attachment to intrinsic nature has been destroyed, as soon as one initiates this contemplation, one must contemplate the ultimate truth.

Although one does not cling to the nature when analyzing it through the four propositions, delusion still persists as one continues to conceptualize its names. Since the principle is not yet seen, this remains merely conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). One must therefore contemplate the true principle of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) to shatter the marks of names; only after the clinging to marks is destroyed is that reality realized. Thus, it is called "shattering marks" within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Alternatively, if one first contemplates the Fourfold Truth by investigating its nature through the four propositions, and thereby realizes that the names of the aggregates, elements, matter, and mind lack the characteristics of the four propositions, this is already termed the "Truth of Reality" (satyadharma) breaking both nature and characteristics. How could one wait until turning to contemplate the breaking of characteristics before employing the Truth of Reality?

If that is so, for what reason does the investigation of nature (svabhāva) state "not from self, other, or both," while the investigation of characteristics (lakṣaṇa) states "not internal, external, or in between"? Since the phrasing of these statements differs, they reveal distinct principles and employ different methods of contemplation.
What is meant by the single four-line contemplation of emptiness that shatters the two kinds of attachment?

Answer: As previously stated, this was explained by way of sequential reference in response to the characteristics of the attachments to be shattered; thus, when investigating their nature, it is said they are "neither self nor other," and when investigating their characteristics, it is said they are "neither internal nor external."
Examining the gateway of contemplation (*guanmen*), how could there be any divergent paths? Thus, Jingxi said:
"Internally, there is only the cause; externally, there is only the condition," and so forth.

Moreover, having completed the explanation of the contemplation on the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), he cites the four lines from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, "All phenomena do not arise from themselves," as proof;
likewise, upon completing the explanation of the contemplation on the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), he again cites those same four lines from that treatise.
Illuminating it with this, there should be no separate contemplation.
Furthermore, if one says that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are merely named as a single, general "contemplation of emptiness," this refers to the "contemplation of the two emptinesses.
Question:
In the *Fahua Shu*, the two emptinesses—of phenomena (*dharmas*) and of persons (*pudgalas*)—are elucidated through the categories of the real and the conventional, and the provisional and the real.
Jingxi’s commentary explains:
“The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the emptiness of phenomena; the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is the emptiness of persons.”

The conventional is provisionally real, yet it leads to the profound text wherein the worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya) refutes intrinsic nature and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) refutes the provisional. The refutation of the provisional serves as proof for the emptiness of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā), while the refutation of intrinsic nature serves as proof for the emptiness of nature (svabhāva-śūnyatā).

If the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) were merely a single contemplation of emptiness, why would one cite the two types of emptiness—of person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—to manifest the two truths?
This is because at the time of the emptiness of person, there is as yet no emptiness of phenomena; thus, there are the two types of emptiness: of nature and of characteristics.

If one follows the analogy that both person and phenomena are empty, then the two types of emptiness ought to be distinct. Why, then, is it said that the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) has not yet been revealed in principle, while there is no separate contemplation for the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?
Answer: When followers of the Hīnayāna attain the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is possible that they have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Just as when the delusions of views are destroyed, one attains the fruit of Srotāpanna, which is called "attaining the emptiness of sentient beings" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
This merely partially reveals the ultimate truth; by further destroying the delusions of thought, one then attains the "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The principle is thoroughly revealed:

in the Mahāyāna, the person, phenomena, and their objects are fused; thus, the path of contemplation is not distinct from them. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The nature of form is like the nature of the self; the nature of the self is like the nature of form."
"The four aggregates are like the self; the application of contemplation is likewise.

Even if there are distinctions between coarse and subtle delusions, or between the prior and subsequent stages of attachment and its destruction, the application of contemplation is necessarily without temporal differentiation."

As for the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) defining the two truths in terms of the emptiness of persons and phenomena, this is done to provisionally distinguish between the true and the conventional in opposition to what is to be refuted; thus, it cites the refutation of intrinsic nature as "emptiness of nature" based on the worldly truth, and the refutation of characteristics as "emptiness of characteristics" based on the ultimate truth as proof.

Regarding the detailed application of the practice of contemplation: one must first dismantle both essence and characteristics within the objects of the self and persons to realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, by relying on both the conventional and the ultimate regarding the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, one investigates these two types of emptiness to exhaustively penetrate this true principle; this is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Only then is the application of the practice of contemplation fully and thoroughly accomplished.

Therefore, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "To seek for a self, a person, or cognitive views within the nature and characteristics [of phenomena] and find them unobtainable is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); to seek for the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases within the nature and characteristics and find them unobtainable is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)."

As for the commentary’s correlation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) with the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is because the essence of this emptiness of persons consists in the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*); thus, conventional truth is employed to manifest the characteristic of this emptiness. Therefore, it is called "conventional and provisional," where "provisional" (*jia*) signifies "illusory" (*mṛṣā*).

If attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is shattered and delusory defilements are thoroughly exhausted, only then is it called the True Truth; thus it is termed "true reality" (*tattva*), where "reality" (*shi*) signifies the ultimate.

Master Jingxi, embodying the intent of this commentary, further employs the *Xuanyu* (Profound Meaning) to take conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) as a means to reveal meanings such as the emptiness of nature (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*), thereby providing proof. Hence he says: "The true and the conventional are non-dual, and the two types of emptiness are simultaneous."
Question:

Since it is said that the two truths are non-dual and the two emptinesses are simultaneous, revealing them to be a single principle and a single emptiness, why then distinguish between the two truths and clarify the two emptinesses?

Answer: In reality, the principle revealed is one, and the contemplation that observes it is also one. However, two types of emptiness are distinguished in order to counteract the attachments of those to be refuted, and they are correlated with the two truths to manifest the varying depths of emptiness.

Therefore, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature and characteristics, "emptiness of nature" refers to principle; since that principle has not yet been manifested, it is merely termed "emptiness clarified through conventional truth.
Because emptiness is still not exhaustive, it is merely termed "emptiness of nature," which nonetheless remains within the realm of worldly phenomena.

Furthermore, one contemplates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) to dismantle the characteristics of this grasping; once these characteristics are dismantled, the principle becomes manifest, which is then termed the ultimate truth. When contemplation is perfected, it is termed the emptiness of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā). Therefore, the two types of emptiness are revealed by means of the two truths.

Therefore, one should know that if the two emptinesses of nature and characteristics are distinguished as true and conventional in relation to what is to be negated, then the two emptinesses of person and phenomena are elucidated by means of the two truths;
this is likewise the case according to principle.

This refers to the emptiness of persons; because this emptiness is not yet ultimate, it is manifested by relying on the conventional, and thus it is said that the conventional truth is the emptiness of persons.
As for the emptiness of phenomena, since this emptiness is already pure, it is manifested by relying on the ultimate, and thus it is said that the ultimate truth is the emptiness of phenomena.

Moreover, although one employs the contemplation of the mutual integration of arising and reality to illuminate the realm where the conventional and the ultimate are non-dual, sentient beings have, since beginningless time, predominantly conceptualized a self within the realm of arising and given rise to attachments therein. Consequently, even this contemplation of non-duality must first apply its function to the realm of arising; thus, when destroying the attachment to a person, it is provisionally termed "emptiness of arising" (pudgala-śūnyatā).

Since the attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) still persists, one must further contemplate that these phenomena are fundamentally non-existent and that this attachment is free from the characteristics of the four extremes; only then is it termed the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
Therefore, the Great Master stated that initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) realizes the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), while ultimate awakening (niṣṭhā-bodhi) realizes the emptiness of phenomena.
However, these two truths manifest the characteristics of the two emptinesses, and the practice and characteristics of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) are likewise the same.

It is simply that, by universally employing contemplation and tranquility to illuminate ultimate truth, it relies upon the conventional and the real to manifest nature and characteristics, clarifying that these two emptinesses reside solely within ultimate truth.

In the teaching of perfect reality, the essence of arising and the essence of dharmas, as well as the investigation of nature and the investigation of characteristics, are exclusively the Middle Way of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Since this Dharma-nature is without arising and without intrinsic nature, it is termed the "conventional truth" that refutes arising and refutes nature.
This birth and this nature are themselves the Dharma; the essence of the Dharma is fundamentally empty, which is termed the "True Truth" that destroys phenomena and destroys marks.
Although it relies upon the two truths, it employs the Middle Way throughout to manifest the two kinds of emptiness.
The Universal [Vehicle] does not possess this contemplation; let students reflect upon it.

However, for a detailed clarification of the two kinds of emptiness—how the grasping at objects and the grasping at a person perish as they follow the perishing of the grasping at phenomena—the full account is as found in the commentary on the "Chapter on Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-parivarta*) in the previous sub-commentary.
3. The two lines beginning with “mad and foolish” refer to ordinary, deluded beings who do not understand the request for [the Buddha] to manifest.

Above, the Buddha’s samādhi of empty wisdom was praised as pervading all realms of existence; therein, all distinctions completely vanish, and only true wisdom remains, free from further defilement or differentiation.

The tree deity understood clearly that ordinary beings were deluded, distracted, and ignorant, failing to realize that both nature (*lakṣaṇa*) and characteristics (*svabhāva*) are empty. Therefore, he requested the Buddha to emerge from meditative absorption.
Second, [the section on] proclaiming his former constant vow and formally requesting him to emerge from absorption has four parts.
First, the five lines beginning with “I have always” formally recount the former vows and practice to manifest the request.
Regarding "I constantly mind the Buddha," "minding" (*nian*) is simply another name for "contemplative observation" (*guanzhao*).
When the mind roams through the Dharma-realm, it constantly illumines the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Because my past power of contemplation was insufficient and I sought to attain profound realization, I supplemented this with vows, joined my palms in prostration, added yearning and weeping, shed tears while practicing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and so forth—all of which assisted the contemplation of constant mindfulness.
What is called "supreme great compassion" is precisely unconditional compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*).
Because it is practiced through the union of the primary and auxiliary practices, it is termed "supreme.
Question:

The tree deity was present at the assembly and clearly saw the Tathāgata entering meditative concentration to preach the sutra; for what reason does he now repeatedly say that he wishes to see the Buddha?
Answer: There are two reasons here.

First, the Tathāgata enters meditative absorption primarily for the purpose of preaching the sūtras; once the preaching is concluded, he must necessarily emerge from that absorption, and to emerge from it, he requires an invitation.
Therefore, when the Buddha emerged from meditative absorption, he was able to certify that what had been said in the three successive rounds was all true.

Once the affairs of this single period were concluded, a tree deity made an earnest request; thus, [the Buddha] recounted his former constant vow to see [the Buddha] again and added further vows and practices, desiring that those in the future might also be able to see the Buddha. Hence it is said: "May my person always be able to see the Buddha."

Second, the tree deity has long been able to perceive the true body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata; desiring to increase his contemplation of the Buddha and further seek supreme realization, he requested the Buddha to emerge from meditative absorption and repeatedly expressed his wish to behold him.

If one succeeds in obtaining the Tathāgata’s response by manifesting his body, then the true Buddha within one's own mind will be further clarified and revealed; therefore, the conclusion below states: "I only pray that, out of compassion, you will manifest your body for me."
2. The second section, "The Convention for Appearing through Compassion," has three parts.
First, the two lines beginning with "World-Honored One" clarify that compassion is able to protect those lost in darkness.
The tree deity was personally unaware of the Tathāgata’s supreme true body; therefore, he requested the Buddha’s empowerment, vowing that his own body might always behold the Buddha.
Furthermore, out of compassion for others who were likewise blinded by delusion and failed to see the Buddha’s true essence, he recounted how the World-Honored One constantly protects all beings.
Therefore, those who thirst and long to see [the Buddha] lead both themselves and others to entreat the Buddha to manifest his body.
Second, the one and a half lines beginning with "śrāvaka" clarify the nature of the noble and the ordinary before they have yet awakened that nature.
The tree deity then struck [the drum] to invite the present Buddha to emerge from meditative absorption.

Although the Buddha remained in samādhi, his nature was clear and pure like lapis lazuli, transparent both inside and out; thus, he perceived the capacities of sentient beings and manifested responses without ever wavering from his tranquil concentration.

Although the Tathāgata has long since attained full clarity, because sentient beings have not yet given rise to the supreme concentration, the tree deity repeatedly requested his appearance to awaken them to this opportunity. He then presented six analogies to demonstrate that the physical body of the śrāvaka is not the essence of luminosity; the true reality they have realized is silent and devoid of cognition, like the emptiness of space, the smoke and flame of a lamp, a magical illusion, an echo in a valley, a transformation produced by supernatural power, or the moon reflected in water—all of which lack substantial nature and cannot be both quiescent and manifest simultaneously.
The nature of sentient beings is illusory and manifests in the present; like what is seen in a dream, it possesses no real characteristic.
Third, regarding the Buddha’s sphere of activity, there is the request for him to manifest his vision.

This clearly explains that the Buddha has entered a meditative concentration endowed with compassionate illumination; therefore, he is requested to emerge from this concentration so that I and the assembly may attain peace and happiness.
3. The following one and a half lines, beginning with "All," express compassion for ordinary beings and sages who do not know how to request the manifestation [of the Buddha].

Because tree spirits and other such beings—ordinary people and lesser sages alike—are deluded regarding the realm where the Buddha dwells, they request that the Buddha manifest his body, thereby causing them to clearly perceive that it is only the mind that manifests as the Buddha.

Regarding the passage on the "immortals with the five supernatural powers" (*pañcābhijña-ṛṣi*): this specifically refers to those within the human realm who, through the mastery of esoteric arts, have attained immortality and developed the five supernormal powers. Although they possess the knowledge of others' minds and the recollection of past lives, they do not know the meditative concentrations in which the Buddha dwells, nor how he illuminates principles and manifests responses without ever departing from the essence of the sentient beings' own minds.

Although the two vehicles of the untainted (anāsrava) possess the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, they are likewise dim regarding the Buddha’s realm of mind-only; therefore, it is said that "they also cannot know.
Fourth, the line beginning with "I now" indicates that, having already attained faith and being free from doubt, [the speaker] requests the manifestation [of the Buddha].
Having finished her account, the tree deity clearly understood the Buddha’s sphere of activity without obstruction.

Although she knew that from the beginning there was neither concealment nor manifestation, she observed that the other members of the assembly were collectively deluded regarding the Buddha’s realm as being subject to actual movement and stillness; therefore, she earnestly requested him to emerge from his meditative absorption, saying, "I pray only that you will, out of compassion, manifest yourself before me."
Question:

Now, since the Buddha enters meditative concentration, preaches the Dharma in response to those addressed, and rises to pay homage to the śarīra—events that are witnessed by all during their coming and going at these times—how could the tree deity know that the Tathāgata was still in concentration and had not yet emerged, such that it would offer its earnest entreaty?
Answer: The tree deity possesses great spiritual power and has long worked alongside the Buddha.
In the past, when he was Liu-shui (Jalavāhana) saving the fish, the tree deity manifested half his body to reveal their number.
Since the Elder has already attained Buddhahood, how could the tree deity still remain stuck in the state of an ordinary being?
Therefore, both his movement and his stillness now serve to support the Buddha’s transformation; how could he not know this?
Moreover, for every emergence from and entry into meditative concentration, there is a prescribed ritual.

Although the Buddha rose, sat, and moved about, he did not manifest the signs of emerging from concentration until the tree deity’s earnest entreaty was most persistent; only then did he manifest the appearance of emerging.

As for its characteristics: one must first observe a slight movement of the body, followed by the exhalation of breath and a slow, deliberate stretching before rising; only then does one know that the Tathāgata has manifested the signs of emerging from meditative concentration.

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of "rising with composure," while this sūtra says "emitting a subtle and wondrous sound"; thus we know that whenever one emerges from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is invariably a corresponding sign.
Question:
The new sūtra itself states: "At that time, the Bhagavat, during the late afternoon, arose from samādhi, surveyed the great assembly, and spoke these verses:"
"The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the wondrous Dharma, is the most supreme king among all sūtras.
Why is it that in the present version of the prophecy (the *Cankben*), it is only after the three rounds of praise have concluded that it says he "arises from samādhi"?
If the interpretations of the translators differ, what can be done about how the compiler arranged the text and its sequence in the Sanskrit original?
Answer: Since the Sanskrit originals themselves differ, why should they need to be reconciled?
As for those students who have no means of understanding this scripture, I shall now briefly attempt an evaluation of it; if it accords with reason, I hope there will be no private reservations.

Now, as for this sutra, ancient masters have maintained that it is a teaching of a specific category (p’ien-fang), namely a discourse delivered at a particular time to suit the capacities of sentient beings; therefore, Tiantai classified it as being subsumed within the Vaipulya (fangděng) division.

This arises from the differentiation of capacities into great and small, and the corresponding response between the provisional and the real: for those who respond to the provisional and the small, it is made to appear that the Buddha emerges from meditative concentration to preach the Dharma; for those who respond to the real and the great, they know that the Buddha remains in concentration while delivering the teaching.

This is also like the account in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where it is described that one enters meditative absorption within the body of a woman and emerges from it to preach the Dharma within the body of a man.

Since the manifestations were diverse according to the specific circumstances of those times, the compilers of the scriptures sometimes state that he first emerged from concentration before preaching, while others say that he emerged from concentration after finishing his preaching.

However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who compiled the sūtras did not follow a single path; there were compilations made both inside and outside of caves, and it is also said that the Sanskrit texts contained various levels of phonetic approximation and precision, resulting in different Sanskrit manuscripts being encountered by the translators.

As Master Xian-chen once traveled through the Five Indias, he must have seen the original Sanskrit text; seeing it stated that the Buddha spoke while in meditative concentration, one must believe and respectfully translate it as such.

Master Jing originally propagated the minor scriptures, but later encountered Sanskrit texts; upon seeing that some stated the Buddha spoke only after arising from meditative concentration, this accorded perfectly with his own school’s tenets, and thus he included it in his compilation without alteration.

When it comes to the enumeration of the assembly of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and others, all state that they arose from meditative concentration at the hour of late afternoon and arrived at the site of the Buddha’s assembly.
Ancient masters have often argued that the translator’s rendering is not elegant or appropriate, and there is indeed some truth to this.
However, the actions of the Sage Teacher were certainly not undertaken in vain; those of ordinary capacity and superficial learning have failed to fully investigate their underlying causes.
To seek out faults and find only faults—to add these superfluous accusations—is already an extreme excess.
Let students embody this and reflect upon it.
Question:
Since the Great Master has already explained the sutra based on the *Chen* manuscript, why does he say, "Entering, one roams within the Dharma-nature; emerging, one narrates the King of Sutras"?

Answer: The Tathāgata always abides in meditative concentration within the dharmatā; yet, in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings and following their needs, he manifests the appearance of entering concentration.
Although his mind dwells in the principle of quiescence, his mouth utters these words; therefore, it is called "Emerging from Concentration to Narrate the King of Sutras."
In essence, tranquility does not obstruct illumination, and discourse does not hinder meditative concentration; it does not mean that the body emerges from concentration.
Fourth, responding to the invitation to arise from concentration, in two parts:
first, the line beginning with "At that time" clarifies that the scribe of the sutra describes the emergence from concentration.

"At that time" refers to the moment when the tree deity had finished her request; the Buddha manifested the signs of emerging from meditative concentration and spoke words of praise with a subtle and wondrous voice, gladdening the fourfold assembly with his refined and exquisite tones.
Second, the two lines beginning with "Excellent" clarify that the Buddha, having arisen from meditative concentration, is able to offer praise.

The Buddha’s praise of the tree deity accords with the preceding two points: because both the bodhisattvas and the wondrous banner (Cāmaradhvaja) are able to praise the teachings spoken by the Buddha, these are all "joyful words."

From the "Introduction Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) onwards, the Tathāgata has clarified the Great Substance, the Great Principle, and the Great Function—these being the three sublime dharmas of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*. Therefore, it is said: "He has well expounded these words."

If sentient beings hear these three dharmas, they will immediately be able to give rise to understanding, realize awakening, and clearly comprehend eternal abiding; therefore, it is said that they have entered the Dharma-gate of the nectar-like state of non-arising.
II. Zhiyi’s General Explanation, in two parts: A.
Explanation based on the meaning, in two parts: 1.
Explanation based on the meaning of the Buddha’s praise, in two parts:
First, praising the cause by means of its resultant fruit, in two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of the meaning of praising the cause, in two parts:
first, indicating the meaning.
The passage beginning with "I say" provides a general explanation.

As for the four sections of the text: the former Master divided the topical outline into only three parts, merging the passage concerning the Tathāgata’s arousal of the three practices into the section on the tree deity; hence the commentary states "and so forth."
Now, it is only through the commentary and exegesis of Zhiyi (Zhang’an) that the principle is fully exhausted; the text is clearly visible [in his works].
Second, citing scriptural evidence.
Second, showing the seal that confirms the praise of the teaching.

In all three sections, the Bodhisattvas first praise the Buddha and then praise the teaching he has expounded; that is, they praise the Tathāgata’s great essence, great wisdom, and great function as revealed from the "Introductory Chapter" onward, which constitute the causes cultivated by Bodhisattvas throughout this sutra.

Why is this? In the "Introductory Chapter," the wandering within the dharma-nature is elucidated; the Buddha points out that what is wandered within are these kings of all sutras. These three sections constitute the general essence of the single sutra spoken by the Buddha.

The "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) clarifies the Buddha’s fruit of permanence; these three sections constitute the Great Wisdom of the Buddha, which is the primary teaching of this sutra—wisdom being its central tenet (*mūla*).

The "Chapter on Repentance" (*Pratideśanā*), the "Chapter on Praise" (*Stuti*), and the "Chapter on Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-parivarta*) represent the Great Function of the Buddha, which is the secondary teaching of this sutra.
From the "Chapter on the Four Kings" to the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body," all these sections expound upon the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the causes [for enlightenment].

Since the three successive praises of the teaching are stated to be the words of the Buddha, the Tathāgata certainly arose to provide his seal of approval, exclaiming: "It is well that the tree deity and others have spoken these words."
Second, praising [the Buddha] through the three karmas.
Zhiyan explains that this chapter clarifies that the resultant Buddha has definitively arisen and is thus able to joyfully proclaim the teachings for the sake of the causal practitioner.
Furthermore, examining the preceding text of the sutra, there is also the meaning of the resultant body paying homage to the śarīra.
"Śarīra" is translated as "bone-fragments," which refers precisely to the physical body.

In the preceding "Chapter on Repentance," the Buddha praised the Great Repentance; in the "Chapter on Praise," the Buddha praised the Dragon Honored One as the Great Praise. That both are termed "Great" is because both the act of repentance and the act of praise are equal to the great essence of the Dharma-nature, through which one realizes that the nature of both sin and merit is empty.

The "Chapter on the Four Kings" is capable of requesting [the teaching], the "Chapter on the Good Collection" is capable of expounding it, the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" and others are capable of listening to it, and the "Chapter on Sacrificing the Body" is capable of practicing it; all of these are "eloquent exponents. Together, they are able to comprehend the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (Golden Light Sūtra) in its three aspects: the essence (*tattva*), the doctrine (*artha*), and the function (*prayojana*). Since these constitute all three categories of dharma, they are all termed "eloquent exponents."
Śraddhālakṣaṇa, the Nāga Honored One, the Four Kings, and others are all persons; therefore, it is said that [the teaching] arises from what is spoken by their mouths.
The character *chàn* (孱) is pronounced with the initial *shì* (士) and the final *xiàn* (限); it means "to manifest."
Since one does not engage in non-virtuous actions of body, speech, or mind, it is said that they are spontaneously established by analogy.
Second, regarding the definition of emergence, there are two parts:
first, posing a question based on arising to lead into the entry.
2. Answering regarding the beginning and end of meditative concentration, in two parts:
first, clarifying abiding in the concentration of the dharma-nature.
Question:
Question: In other sutras, one must first enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and only upon emerging from it does one speak;
why, then, does this present sutra always remain in concentration while speaking? Answer:
If one discusses the concentration of the dharma-nature, how could there be any distinction between entering and emerging, or speaking and remaining silent?
Since he manifested this concentration, it was surely to accord with the capacities of sentient beings; for the inclinations and preferences of those capacities differ.

The various sūtras demonstrate that all Buddhas of the past first entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), traversed the conditions of the Dharma, and then, in order to counteract the distracted mind that falsely imagines there is something to be said, they necessarily entered concentration; only upon arising from concentration did they speak.
The fact that this sutra is able to be preached while remaining in meditative concentration from beginning to end signifies that its intent accords with the principle.

Furthermore, it demonstrates that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is immeasurably profound, sovereign, unimpeded, quiescently illuminating, and all-pervading; thus, by stating that [the Buddha] definitively arose [from concentration], it serves as a seal of confirmation for the threefold joyful reception of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.
Second, to reveal the perfect interfusion of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
To say that "if one enters the Dharma-nature" is to manifest that the principle is all-encompassing and does not obstruct coming or going.

Previously, it was proclaimed that the Dharma-nature is immeasurable and profoundly deep; whether one comes out or enters, whether there is speech or silence—how could this ever transcend the Dharma-nature?
Therefore, it is said that the dharma-nature is sovereign.
As for the "four Buddhas," these refer to the Buddhas of the four directions.
The "five Buddhas" include Śākyamuni as well.

Regarding "the same place, various places, and so forth": although the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa and Vulture Peak Mountain differ, for one who realizes that all is mind-only, they see only the wondrous land; thus, the assembly of disciples is one, and the five Buddhas share the same location, possessing a single body and a single wisdom. In this way, the four [Buddhas] have no coming or going, and the one has no abiding.

Those who adhere to the provisional teachings hold various differing views; they claim that the abode of Wondrous Banner is separated from Mount Grdhrakūṭa by many *li*. Therefore, they maintain that the four or five Buddhas do not merely reside in different locations, but also possess distinct bodies and distinct wisdoms, and that they truly come and go, truly dwelling and remaining in fixed places.
Although these distinctions exist, they do not depart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); therefore, it is said that whatever one perceives is entirely without obstruction.
Second, the explanation according to contemplation has two parts:
first, clarifying the objective realms of the three karmas of phenomena.
The phrase "observing the mind" (guānxīn) serves to clarify the explanation of contemplation (guān).
First, it clarifies that the praise offered by the various bodhisattvas—performed through the three karmas—is the object of wondrous contemplation.
Although the praise resides in the mouth, the body must be reverent and the mind must remain respectful; only when the three karmas operate in unison is the meaning of praise fully realized.
II. Clarifying the Three Contemplations of Principle (Li). This has two parts:
first, clarifying the contemplation of principle within phenomena.

Regarding the "three contemplations of mind," this refers to the three contemplations of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle that are able to contemplate, which are illustrated by means of the objects such as the body.
Recently, there have been lecturers who, being unaware of this, claim that later generations arbitrarily added the character "mind" (心).
This is also due to the previous confusion of taking the mind as the object of contemplation, which led to such inconsistencies.
Such errors and fallacies are beyond description.

For instance, the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra* fundamentally clarifies the contemplation of the Buddha, yet the commentary states that "contemplation by means of the mind is its core principle. Failing to grasp this intent, some have recklessly engaged in forced and artificial interpretations.
Students of the present day should reflect upon this with great earnestness.

Regarding the observation that the body cannot be found as a body: first, clarify the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*). By investigating and analyzing the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), one finds they possess no substantial nature; this is called the emptiness of the body's nature (*kāya-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
That which exists merely as a name is the characteristic of the body (*kāya-lakṣaṇa*).

Names are of many kinds; for now, let us cite the six perfections and the ten perfections, etc. Thus: bodily practice of giving is called *dāna*; bodily abstention from all that is improper is called *śīla*; bodily endurance of humiliation is called *kṣānti*; bodily diligent exertion is called *vīrya*; bodily ability to remain tranquil is called *dhyāna*; bodily realization of the emptiness of essence is called *prajñā*; bodily practice of skillful means is called *upāya*; bodily establishment of vows is called *praṇidhāna*; bodily benefiting others is called *bala*; and bodily emergence from birth and death is called *jñāna*.

From the body up to the eighty thousand *rajas* of dharma-gates of bodily activity, the practitioner receives their names accordingly; yet they penetrate that names have no inherent name, and thus the characteristics of the named body are empty.

Although one investigates and examines their nature and characteristics and finds them empty, the various dharmas of form and mind remain vividly present. Therefore, emptiness is not fixed as empty, and the provisional is not fixed as provisional; that which is neither empty nor provisional is the true, wondrous nature, which is called the manifestation of the Middle Way.
Since the observation of the body is thus established, the mouth and mind are understood by analogy.
Second, explaining that the phenomena are attained and the principle is accomplished, in three parts:
first, explaining the failure resulting from the absence of both [observation and contemplation].

Taking the body and so forth as objects, one is able to give rise to contemplation; when contemplation is perfected, the object appears and both phenomena and principle become clearly manifest—this can be understood by comparing it to a pig rubbing against a mountain of gold.
Second, taking clothing and other items as examples.
The three robes are the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, and the antarvāsaka.
The six articles include these, along with the niṣīdana, the pātra, and the water-strainer.
Thus we know that outside the six [inner robes] there are no three;
it is just as with the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, where outside the samādhis there are no dhyānas.
This is because the name "robe" (yi) is restrictive in scope, whereas the name "article" (wu) is somewhat more general.
"Robe" (*cīvara*) carries the meaning of "covering"; since items such as the *pātra* (alms bowl) do not provide covering, they are collectively termed "objects.

This is also like the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*), where feeling, perception, and volition have ceased; thus, the specific names for their constituent factors—such as joy and bliss—are absent, and they are collectively designated by the general term "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*).

Although the four locations within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) all pertain to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), they receive the specific designation of "dhyāna" only when sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) still function.

Thus, one should know that if one understands this, both the three matters and the six principles will be clear; if one is ignorant of it, both the three, the six, the four, and the eight will remain obscure.
Third, the attainment of both principle and phenomena is established together.

The objective realm is manifested through contemplation; when the contemplation of principle is perfected, the three—body, speech, and mind—are termed "wondrous form and mind. Therefore, they are also called the "six contemplations," and this is termed the "accomplishment of phenomena and principle."
The phrase "neither six nor three" refers to the passage in the aforementioned model that was not understood;
this is evident.
In the past, I received the teachings from the Great Master Fazhi, who once composed commentaries during his lectures to explain the sutras and their sub-commentaries.
When he had just finished seventeen chapters, he passed away into tranquility.

As for his final chapter, "Praise of the Buddha," the purport of the sutra is profound and remote, and the structural outline of the commentary remains concise; thus, to unravel its deep-seated mysteries is truly difficult.
Although I am not gifted, I have had the honor of being closely associated with the instruction for a long time; I have therefore compiled my former notes and appended them to the end of this volume.
It is my hope that readers will not cast upon me the reproach of "adding a weasel's tail to a fox's," which signifies a vulgar imitation.
